1.title: The cost barrier
1.assumption: We believed that affordability of activities available in Singapore was the main barrier, and that removing the cost would lead to full participation.
1.reality: Most of these activities are already funded by donors, so cost was rarely the reason families didn't show up. Families would agree to attend, then cancel last minute because of a sick child or a job that came up without much notice.
1.quote: People pay tickets for the beneficiaries to come, they don't come... 20 something people said they would come, 1 family turned up. And they charted a whole bus, a 40-seater bus to bring everyone.
1.transcript:
Now, if you talk about excursions, one of the biggest headaches we get — and we would know this because we run fundraisers, right? Like we're running a Snow White and Seven Dwarfs Wild Rice, then we got Mandeville Music Conservatory concert. People pay for tickets for the beneficiaries to come. They don't come. I can tell you, Campus Impact, so sweet, they invited all of them. I think 40 people, or 20-something people said they would come. One family turned up. And they chartered a whole bus, a 40-seater bus to bring everyone.

The problem is that — that's what we face. That they are thrown so many things, right? And also that — it's not their fault, no — that day, right, family of six, one day one person falls sick, can't wake up. Imagine if you are in a small house, right, say a size of this, maybe slightly bigger, and there are 6 to 11 people staying, right? And it's a lot of chaos, right? And organisation of time and things may not always be on their side.

You can say unreliable, but not because of their fault, but because of many circumstances that make them... Like even jobs, it's so hard to find a job, because if I can work part-time and you need part-time work, right, the women, then they get a job, then one kid falls ill, or all the kids fall ill, who's gonna look after? So they cannot attend the job, and then they get not a good mark. Really multiple issues that face them.

2.title: What parents prioritise
2.assumption: We believed that because parents wanted their kids to have the same opportunities as other children, enrichment activities would rank high on their list of priorities.
2.reality: For many low-income families, bills and food come first. Enrichment is a luxury. It's only once those immediate needs are covered that there's mental space left to think about enrichment for their kids.
2.quote: They are just trying to survive and put bread on the table. What will really help them more is someone who can babysit (their) kids, then (they) can go and work a shift.
2.transcript: Beneficiaries have the luxury of many programs to attend, but they have a lot of things that is happening in their lives. For them, sending their kids to enrichment class weekly at the same time is actually very, very, very difficult. They're just trying to survive, and put bread on table. What will really help them more is someone who can babysit my kids, then I can go and work a shift.

3.title: One-off vs ongoing
3.assumption: Activities like coding classes, zoo trips, and weekend workshops provide valuable enrichment for kids.
3.reality: Although parents showed enthusiasm about these activities, creating real impact requires long-term, regular attendance, not just one-offs. Volunteers will also be needed to track children's progress and provide specialised support.
3.quote: ...this is very one-off and we are in the business of creating more longer-term impact with the children...They have to regularly come for at least like six months.
3.transcript: I don't think this is something you would do, because this is very one-off, and we are in the business of creating more longer-term impact with the children. Ours is a curriculum, so we can't just have a child come one week and not come another week. They have to regularly come for at least like six months.

4.title: Online vs in-person
4.assumption: We believed that creating an online platform offering subsidised and free activities would close the gap in opportunities between low-income kids and their peers.
4.reality: Putting activities online doesn't solve the problem on its own. Families are supported by a network of donors, volunteers, social service organisations (SSOs), and social workers who stay in close, personal contact, providing empathy and encouragement no platform can offer.
4.quote: The programs I run work through communities...If you're going to do this, one way is through the social worker or the SSO, the contact point that's actually seeing the family.
4.transcript: For the programs that I run regularly is working through communities. So the communities select their child. So CDAC selects the children. MSF selects the children. Shine selects the children. Yeah, it's all free for the beneficiaries, all free, but, but it's funded by someone. So all of our programs are funded by donors, whether from foundations or individual donors. Yeah. If you were going to do this, one way is to get through the social worker or the SSO, the the the the the so-called the contact point that is seeing the family, so that they can present like, 'Would you like this? Do you like this?' Yeah.
